items: Open **chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=91**. Keep the **Guided** tab selected (top right).
Read slides 1–12 with **Next**. On slide 9, open **Choose a Substance** and pick **Water**.
Check that **Ice mass** (under the flame slider) reads **7 g**. Do not press ◄◄ or ►► yet.
Move the **Heat** (flame) slider slowly to the right until the ice has completely melted. Stop there.

items.prompt: When ice melts at 0 °C, will its entropy go up or down? Explain with particles.
items.answer: Up. Molecules in the liquid can move and arrange themselves in many more ways than in the solid. Accept: more disorder / more dispersed / more possible arrangements.

items: The First Law: energy cannot be created or {{destroyed}}, only transferred.
The Second Law: the disorder of the universe is always {{increasing}}. In practice, energy cannot be transferred with {{100%}} efficiency.
{{Entropy}} is the disorder of a system. It is related to the number of different {{ways}} the system can arrange its particles.
Balls in a box: making the box smaller, so the balls have fewer places to be, is a {{decrease}} in entropy.
Entropy has the symbol {{S}}. Standard entropy, S°, is based on the {{mole}}.
The sim writes entropy units as {{J/°C}}. AP uses J/K. A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, so the numbers are the same.
For a reversible process, ΔS = {{q / T}}, where q is the heat added and T is the temperature in {{kelvin}}.
When melting begins, the entropy change is {{positive}}. Molecules {{disperse}} a little in the liquid state.
ΔSₘₑₗₜ = q / T(melt) = m(ΔH of fusion) / T(melt)

items.prompt: The sim says water's heat of fusion is 333 J/g. Before the ΔSₘₑₗₜ box fills in, calculate q and ΔSₘₑₗₜ for melting 7 g of ice at 0 °C.
items.answer: q = m·ΔH(fusion) = 7 g × 333 J/g = **2331 J**. T(melt) = 0 + 273 = **273 K**. ΔSₘₑₗₜ = 2331 J / 273 K = 8.5 → **9 J/K** (the sim shows 9 J/°C).

items.prompt: The temperature stayed at 0 °C the whole time the ice melted, yet the entropy went up. Use the sim to explain where the entropy increase came from.
items.answer: Heat (2331 J) went into breaking the solid's order, not into raising T. The molecules went from a fixed lattice to a liquid where they disperse, so there are more ways to arrange them. Accept: q > 0 at constant T so ΔS = q/T > 0; solid → liquid = more disorder.

blocks.text: Press ►► until Ice mass reads 15 g (go back to the start of the heat slider first if the buttons are gone). Predict ΔSₘₑₗₜ, then check. (Answer: 15 × 333 / 273 = 18 J/K. Doubling the mass about doubles ΔS: entropy is extensive.)

items: Continue from the previous section: **Water**, **Ice mass 7 g**.
Keep moving the **Heat** slider to the right, slowly, all the way to the end (vapor at 120 °C). Watch the equation panel change from fusion, to heating, to vaporization.
At the end, press **Next** to load **Ethanol**, then **Acetone**. Each time, check Ice mass still reads **7 g** and run the slider to the end again.

items.prompt: Which step will give water the biggest ΔS: melting, heating the liquid, boiling, or heating the vapor? Why?
items.answer: Boiling. Liquid → gas spreads the molecules out the most, and it takes the most heat (2230 J/g). Accept any answer with a reason; this is a prediction.

items: To heat the liquid, the sim uses the {{average}} of the initial and final temperatures (in K) as T.
The heat for a temperature change is the {{Sensible Heat}}: q = m·Cw·(T₂ − T₁), where Cw is the {{specific heat}}.
When heating the vapor, Cw is the specific heat in the {{gaseous}} state.
Water's heat of vaporization in the sim is {{2230}} J/g.
During vaporization, molecules spread all over the place, so disorder and entropy {{increase}}.
Entropy increases with {{temperature}} and with a change of state from solid to liquid to {{gas}}. It would {{decrease}} if the reverse happened.
ΔS = q / T(avg) = m·Cw·(T₂ − T₁) / ((T₂ + T₁)/2)
ΔSᵥₐₚ = q / T(boil) = m(ΔH of vaporization) / T(boil)
ΔSₜₒₜₐₗ = ΔSₘₑₗₜ + ΔSᵥₐₚ + ΔS (heating legs)

items.prompt: Before the sim shows them, calculate for 7 g of water: (a) ΔS for heating the liquid from 273 K to 373 K (Cw = 4.2 J/g·°C), and (b) ΔSᵥₐₚ for boiling at 373 K.

blocks.note: All values in J/K (the sim prints J/°C). Read ΔS liquid at the end of the liquid leg (or from the ( ) in the ΔSₜₒₜₐₗ row) and ΔS vapor at 120 °C. The ΔSₜₒₜₐₗ row rounds the vapor value to 1.

blocks.prompt: Shape only: sketch the entropy of the 7 g of water as it is heated from 273 K to 393 K. Mark where it melts and where it boils.
blocks.answer: A curve that rises gently while each phase heats, with a vertical jump at 273 K (melting, small) and a much taller vertical jump at 373 K (boiling, about 4–5 times bigger). It never goes down.

items.prompt: Claim and evidence: which process raises entropy the most, for every substance in your table? Explain why at the particle level.
items.answer: Vaporization (ΔSᵥₐₚ is the largest number in each row: 42, 17, 11 J/K). Going from liquid to gas spreads the molecules over a much larger volume, so the number of possible arrangements increases the most.

items.prompt: Water's total ΔS (61 J/K) is much larger than acetone's (25 J/K) for the same mass. Use the table to say which step causes most of the difference.
items.answer: Vaporization: 42 vs 11 J/K. Water's heat of vaporization (2230 J/g) is much larger than acetone's (518 J/g) because of its hydrogen bonds. Accept: stronger IMFs → more heat per gram → bigger ΔS.

pages.title: Absolute Entropy and Entropy of Reaction

items: Open **chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=92** in **Guided**. Press **Next** past the two slides about Gibbs Free Energy.
Open **Choose a Compound** and pick **NH3** (N₂ + 3H₂ ⟶ 2NH₃). Press **Next** until the atoms can move.
Drag each atom toward its partner (follow the ▶▶▶ arrows) to make N₂ and three H₂. Then drag one reactant molecule toward another to make NH₃.
After NH₃, use **Choose a Compound** again for **HCl**, then **NaOH**, and build each one the same way.

items.prompt: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). Will ΔS° be positive or negative? Count moles of gas.
items.answer: Negative: 4 mol of gas → 2 mol of gas, so fewer particles and fewer arrangements.

items: Same as enthalpy, every compound has an {{Entropy}} of formation and a {{Gibbs Free Energy}} of formation. (AP calls the table's entropy values standard molar entropies, S°.)
The Gibbs Free Energy of formation of a pure element such as N₂ or H₂ is {{0}}.
When you make the second and third H₂, the S° value is multiplied by the number of {{moles}}, so the equation shows 3(130.6).
The difference between the products' and the reactants' values is the entropy (and Gibbs) of {{reaction}}.
For NH₃, entropy decreases because all components are {{gaseous}} and there are more {{molecules}} on the reactant side.
Entropy changes with the number of {{molecules}} in gaseous reactions, with the {{temperature}}, and with the change of physical state.
ΔS°rx = Σ n·S°(products) − Σ n·S°(reactants)
ΔG°rx = Σ n·ΔG°f(products) − Σ n·ΔG°f(reactants)

items.prompt: After you make the reactants (but before NH₃), use the table: S°(N₂) = 191.5 and S°(H₂) = 130.6 J/K·mol. The sim will show S°(NH₃) = 192.5 and ΔG°f(NH₃) = −16.7 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔS°rx and ΔG°rx.
ΔS° for NaOH is the most negative in your table. Na(s) and NaOH(s) are solids. Explain the sign using the states of matter.
items.answer: Reactants include 2 mol of gas (O₂ and H₂); the only product is a solid. Losing all the gas means far fewer arrangements, so ΔS° is very negative (−309.4 J/K). Accept: gas → solid.

items.prompt: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl has 2 mol of gas on each side. Why is its ΔS° so small (+20.1 J/K)?
items.answer: The number of gas molecules does not change, so the disorder changes only a little. Accept: same moles of gas → ΔS near zero.

items: Open **chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=93** in **Guided**. The temperature starts at **298 K**. Read the two intro slides with **Next**.
Each round: click bottle **A**, set the **ΔH°** slider and let go to lock it, set the **ΔS°** slider and let go, then click bottle **B**.

Use these values. Each slider starts on them; click the slider knob and let go without moving it. Round 1: ΔH° **−2500 J/mol**, ΔS° **+25 J/(mol·K)**. Round 2: **+5000**, **+16**. Round 3: **−5000**, **−16**. Round 4: **+2500**, **−25**.
Round 2: drag **Temperature** up to **320 K**. Round 3 starts at 320 K: drag it down to **298 K**. Then press **Next** to watch the reaction.

items.prompt: Round 1 has ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0. Will ΔG° be positive or negative? Does the temperature matter?
items.answer: Negative at every temperature: ΔH° is negative and −TΔS° is also negative, so both terms push ΔG° below zero.

items: ΔG° = ΔH° − {{TΔS°}}, where T is the temperature in kelvin.
ΔG° tells you which direction is {{thermodynamically favored}} under standard conditions. A favored reaction is also called {{spontaneous}}.
ΔG° does not tell you how {{fast}} a reaction occurs. Even a favorable reaction can be very {{slow}}.
A reaction with a negative ΔG° is called {{exergonic}}. A reaction with a positive ΔG° is called {{endergonic}}.
In rounds 2 and 3, ΔH° and ΔS° stay {{fixed}}. Only {{T}} changes.
The crossover temperature is specific to the model reaction. With ΔG° this close to zero, a real mixture would stop partway, at {{equilibrium}}.

items.prompt: Round 1, before you click B: calculate ΔG° at 298 K.
Round 2, before you click B: calculate ΔG° at 298 K, and the temperature where ΔG° = 0.

blocks.note: In round 1 the sim keeps the ΔG° box empty until the reaction is complete; it is the same value as your calculation. Rounds 2 and 3 show a Start / Now strip under the equation.

blocks.prompt: Using your round 2 numbers (+232 J/mol at 298 K, −120 J/mol at 320 K), sketch ΔG° vs. T. Mark where the line crosses zero and label the favorable side.
blocks.answer: A straight line sloping down (slope = −ΔS° = −16 J/mol·K), crossing ΔG° = 0 at 312.5 K. Above 312.5 K (ΔG° < 0) is labeled favorable.

items.prompt: Round 3 is exothermic (ΔH° < 0), but at 320 K it was not favored. Use ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° to explain why cooling made it favorable.
items.answer: ΔS° is negative, so −TΔS° is positive and grows with T. At 320 K, +5120 outweighs −5000, so ΔG° = +120. Cooling to 298 K shrinks the −TΔS° term to +4768, so ΔG° = −232 J/mol. Accept: the entropy term wins at high T, the enthalpy term wins at low T.

items.prompt: Explain why no temperature can make round 4 favorable.
items.answer: ΔH° is positive and ΔS° is negative, so −TΔS° is also positive. Both terms are positive at every positive T, so ΔG° is always positive.

items.prompt: The sim does not show K here. Use K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), to find K for round 1 (−9950 J/mol, 298 K) and round 3 (−232 J/mol, 298 K). What does K ≈ 1 mean?
items.answer: Round 1: K = e^(9950 / (8.314 × 298)) = e^4.02 = **55**. Round 3: K = e^(232 / 2478) = e^0.094 = **1.10**. K ≈ 1 means reactants and products are both present in similar amounts at equilibrium; the reaction is barely favored and would not go to completion.

blocks.text: Free Explore: set ΔH° = +5000 and ΔS° = +16, then move the temperature back and forth across 312.5 K.

items: Open **chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=94** in **Guided**.
Open **Choose a Reaction** and pick **Zn(s) + Cu+2(aq) ⇌ Zn+2(aq) + Cu(s)**. Use only this reaction for the rest of the worksheet.

Press **Next** to read. When asked: click the **Zn²⁺** bottle (first beaker), then the **Cu²⁺** bottle, then click the **Cu electrode** to push it down. Stop when the sim asks you to plug in the Voltmeter.

items.prompt: In this cell, which metal do you think will lose electrons (be oxidized)? Which electrode will gain mass?
items.answer: Zn is oxidized (Zn → Zn²⁺), so the zinc electrode loses mass; Cu²⁺ is reduced onto the copper electrode, so it gains mass. Accept any answer with a reason; this is a prediction.

items: An electrochemical cell is, in other words, a {{battery}}.
{{Reduction}} happens when a species gains electrons. {{Oxidation}} happens when a species loses electrons.
Redox reactions are {{reversible}} reactions, so they go towards {{equilibrium}}.
Q = [Zn²⁺] / [Cu²⁺]. After both solutions are poured, each is {{1.00}} M, so Q = {{1.00}}.
The {{anode}} is the zinc bar because it is oxidized. The {{cathode}} is the copper bar because it is reduced.
The salt bridge keeps both solutions {{neutral}}, so the reaction lasts longer.
Electrons flow from the {{negative}} side (anode) to the positive side (cathode).
Anode (oxidation): Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + {{2e⁻}}
Cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → {{Cu(s)}}
Cell notation: {{Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu}}

items.prompt: The Q expression on screen has only [Zn²⁺] and [Cu²⁺]. Why are Zn(s) and Cu(s) left out?
items.answer: They are pure solids; their activity is constant (1), so they do not appear in Q or K.

items.prompt: What would happen to the cell if the salt bridge were removed? Use the sim's description of what the bridge does.
items.answer: The anode beaker would build up positive charge (Zn²⁺) and the cathode beaker negative charge, so electron flow would quickly stop. The salt bridge keeps both solutions neutral. Accept: the battery wouldn't last / current stops.

pages.title: Cell Potential, Free Energy and K

items: Continue with **Zn/Cu**. Drag the **Voltmeter** onto the middle of the cable. Later, drag the **Thermometer** into the solution.
When the sim says to run the reaction, press **▶ Play the reaction** (under the graph) or drag the dot along the curve. Stop at "Equilibrium has been reached!".

items.prompt: Before you plug in the voltmeter: the sim uses E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. Calculate E°cell.
items.answer: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = **+1.10 V**

items.prompt: Calculate ΔG° in kJ (n = 2, F = 96485 C/mol).
Before you add the thermometer: calculate K at 298 K from ΔG° = −RT ln K (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)).

items: The voltmeter measures the {{Cell Potential}} (Ecell). Under standard conditions it is called the Standard Cell Potential, E°cell.
F is Faraday's constant, the charge in one mole of electrons: {{96485}} C/mol.
When ΔG = 0 the reaction is at {{equilibrium}}. When ΔG < 0 the {{forward}} reaction proceeds; when ΔG > 0 the {{reverse}} reaction proceeds.
The thermometer reads {{298}} K. K is huge, so at equilibrium there are many more {{products}} than reactants.
Nernst equation: right now Ecell equals E°cell because the conditions are still {{standard}}.
On the graph, the slope of the curve at each point is ΔG. At the bottom (Q = K) the slope is {{0}}.
ΔG° = −nFE°cell
ΔG° = −RT ln K
ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q
Ecell = E°cell − (RT/nF) ln Q

blocks.prompt: Shape only (the sim's graph is not to scale): sketch free energy G as the reaction runs from reactants to products. Mark where Q = K.
blocks.answer: A curve that falls steeply from the reactant side to a minimum close to the products side, then rises a little. The minimum is Q = K, where the slope (ΔG) is zero.

items.prompt: At equilibrium the voltmeter read 0.00 V. Explain, using Q and K, why a battery "dies".
items.answer: As the cell runs, [Zn²⁺] rises and [Cu²⁺] falls, so Q grows toward K. At Q = K, ΔG = 0 and Ecell = 0: no more driving force, no current. A dead battery is a cell at equilibrium.

items.prompt: E°cell, ΔG° and K all point the same way for this cell. Give the sign or size of each and say what they mean.
items.answer: E°cell = +1.10 V (positive), ΔG° = −212 kJ (negative), K = 1.6 × 10³⁷ (much greater than 1). All three say the forward reaction is thermodynamically favored and strongly product-favored.

items.prompt: Hypothetical (not in the sim): a Zn/Cu cell has [Zn²⁺] = 2.0 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M. Use the Nernst equation to find Ecell at 298 K. Is it more or less than 1.10 V?

items: Continue with **Zn/Cu** at equilibrium. When asked, click the **Zn²⁺** bottle to shake more Zn²⁺ into the first beaker.
When asked to run the reverse reaction, press **▶ Play the reaction** or drag the dot back to equilibrium.
Drag the **Power Source** onto the cell. Set the **I — current** slider to **5.0 A**. **Stop and do the calculation below.** Then set the **t — time** slider to **1800 s**.

items.prompt: Zn²⁺ is a product. If you add more Zn²⁺ at equilibrium, which way will the reaction go?
items.answer: Backward (toward reactants): adding product makes Q > K, so the reverse reaction is favored (Le Châtelier).

items: After shaking in more Zn²⁺, ΔG is {{positive}} and Ecell is {{negative}}: the forward reaction is not favored right now.
Looking at it as the reverse reaction, the electrodes swap roles: Cu(s) is now the {{anode}} and Zn(s) the cathode, and E°cell = {{−1.10}} V.
A cell where a redox reaction happens spontaneously and produces an electric current is a {{Galvanic}} or Voltaic cell.
In an {{Electrolytic}} cell, an electric current has to be supplied so the {{non-spontaneous}} reaction proceeds.
Knowing I (current) and t (time), we can calculate q, the {{charge}} in coulombs. Dividing q by Faraday's constant gives the moles of {{e⁻}}.
In electrolysis the zinc electrode gets {{coated}} with zinc instead of being consumed. This is often used for coating one metal with another.

blocks.note: Read Ecell and ΔG from the equation strip. The voltmeter itself keeps reading −0.01 V until the reverse run reaches equilibrium.

items: q = I × t
moles e⁻ = q / F
moles Zn = moles e⁻ / {{2}}
mass Zn = M × moles Zn   (M = 65.38 g/mol)

items.prompt: Before you set the time: calculate the mass of Zn plated by 5.0 A for 1800 s.

blocks.prompt: Shape only (the sim's graph is not to scale): sketch the mass of each electrode during electrolysis.
blocks.answer: Zn electrode: straight line going up. Cu electrode: straight line going down. Both linear, because a constant current moves electrons at a constant rate.

items.prompt: The same number of moles of Cu dissolves as Zn plates (0.047 mol). Cu's molar mass is 63.55 g/mol. Is the mass of Cu lost the same as the mass of Zn gained? Show your work.
items.answer: No. Cu lost = 0.0466 × 63.55 = **2.96 g**, Zn gained = 3.05 g. Equal moles (both 2e⁻ per atom), but different molar masses, so different grams.

items.prompt: Compare the galvanic cell you built earlier with the electrolytic cell. For each, give the direction of the reaction and the sign of ΔG.
items.answer: Galvanic: forward reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, ΔG < 0, the cell produces current. Electrolytic: reverse reaction Zn²⁺ + Cu → Zn + Cu²⁺, ΔG > 0, an outside power source must push it.

blocks.text: Free Explore: pick Sn(s) + Cu+2(aq). Predict E°cell (0.34 − (−0.14) = 0.48 V) and ΔG° (−93 kJ) before you check. Then try 5.0 A for 1800 s: Sn has M = 118.71 g/mol, so more grams (5.54 g) plate for the same charge.

conclusion.prompt: Link the unit together: for the Zn/Cu cell, E°cell = +1.10 V. What does this tell you about ΔG°, K and thermodynamic favorability? Does it tell you how fast the cell reacts? Use a sentence from the Gibbs lab.
conclusion.answer: E° > 0 → ΔG° = −nFE° = −212 kJ < 0 → K = 1.6 × 10³⁷ ≫ 1: the forward reaction is thermodynamically favored and product-favored. It says nothing about rate: "ΔG° does not tell you how fast it occurs; even a favorable reaction can be very slow."

conclusion.prompt: Use the sim's NH₃ numbers: ΔS°rx = −198.3 J/K and ΔG°rx = −33.4 kJ at 298 K. Find ΔH°rx. Then find the temperature above which making NH₃ is no longer favored (assume ΔH° and ΔS° stay constant). Which sign case from the Gibbs lab is this?
conclusion.answer: ΔH° = ΔG° + TΔS° = −33.4 + (298)(−0.1983) = **−92.5 kJ**. ΔG° = 0 at T = ΔH°/ΔS° = −92.5 / −0.1983 = **466 K**; above that it is unfavorable. ΔH° < 0, ΔS° < 0: the round 3 case, favorable at low T.

conclusion.prompt: Every lab in this unit had something increasing or decreasing toward a limit: entropy during heating, ΔG° during a temperature change, Ecell during the run. Explain why the voltmeter reached 0.00 V while the entropy of the heated water kept rising.
conclusion.answer: The cell reaction moves toward equilibrium, where ΔG = 0 and Ecell = 0, and then stops. The water was being given heat from outside at every step, so its entropy kept increasing (ΔS = q/T > 0 for each step). Accept: the cell is a closed reaction reaching equilibrium; the heating is driven by an outside energy source.

key_notes: **Unit 9 is not in the site catalog.** The four labs ship in the deployed Thermodynamics Lab bundle but appear only by direct URL: chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=91 … ?part=94 (add &mode=freeExplore for Free Explore). They are not on the sim's home page or its menu drawer, and the site's AP Unit 9 list is empty.

**Units:** Part 91 writes entropy in J/°C (same numbers as J/K). Part 92's narration says ΔG°f is in J and the beaker callout shows S° values as "kJ"; the table values are really S° in J/K·mol and ΔG°f in kJ/mol. Part 93 uses J/mol and J/(mol·K) (AP problems usually give ΔH° in kJ: remind students to convert). The worksheet uses J/K and kJ/mol.
**Part 91 mass setting changes every answer.** Ice mass defaults to 7 g (range 5–20 g). All Part 91 answers are for 7 g. The original slide deck's 18 / 90 / 130 J/°C are for 15 g.
**Part 91 uses T(K) = T(°C) + 273** (not 273.15) and ΔS = q/T(avg) for heating legs. The exact value is m·c·ln(T₂/T₁): 9.18 J/K for the water liquid leg, versus the sim's 9.10. Accept the sim's 9.
**Part 91 water data:** c(liquid) 4.2, c(vapor) 1.9 J/g·°C, ΔH(vap) 2230 J/g (textbooks: 4.184, 2.0, 2260).
**Part 92 S° and ΔG°f values match standard tables** to within 0.3. 2Na is one row with S° = 102.6 (2 × 51.3). The table heads the S° column "ΔS°f"; AP calls these standard molar entropies.

**Part 93 values are invented model numbers** for a hypothetical A + B → C (the worksheet says so). In Guided mode students choose the slider magnitudes; the Set Up box names the default values so everyone's table matches. Round 2 accepts only ΔS° = 15 or 16 at ΔH° = +5000; round 3 accepts 16–17.

**Part 93 temperature carries over** from round 2 into round 3. If a student stops round 2 at 313 K instead of 320 K, round 3 starts at +8 J/mol and their round-2 final ΔG° is −8 J/mol. Both are correct for their T.
**Part 94: use only Zn/Cu for graded work.** The Al/Ag option labels Ag⁺ as "Ag+3" / [Ag³⁺], writes Q without the cube on [Ag⁺], and the half-reaction text uses n = 3 as each ion's charge.

**Part 94 numbers:** E° = 1.10 V, ΔG° = −212 kJ, K shown as 1.6×10³⁷ (R = 8.314, T = 298 K). The disturbance multiplies Q by 2.5, giving Ecell −0.01 V and ΔG +2 kJ. Electrolysis: I = 1–10 A (0.5 A steps), t = 100–3600 s (100 s steps).
**Part 94 Faraday rounding:** for 5.0 A × 1800 s the strip prints 3.05 = 65.38 x 0.047, but 65.38 × 0.047 = 3.07. The sim multiplies the unrounded moles (0.04664). Accept 3.05–3.07 g.
**The free-energy graph (Part 94) and the mass–time graph are schematic.** The worksheet asks only for their shapes.
AP topics 9.4 (kinetic control) and 9.6 (coupled reactions) are not covered by the sim; see the lesson plan's prep.

ap_topics: 9.3 Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability
9.4 Thermodynamic and Kinetic Control (one sentence only: ΔG° does not give the rate)
9.5 Free Energy and Equilibrium (ΔG° = −RT ln K in Part 94; K from ΔG° as a worksheet calculation)
lesson_plan.sim_location: Thermodynamics Lab, Unit 9 parts, by direct link only: chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=91 (entropy), ?part=92 (absolute entropy), ?part=93 (Gibbs), ?part=94 (electrochemistry). Add &mode=freeExplore for Free Explore.
lesson_plan.essential_question: How do entropy, enthalpy and temperature decide whether a reaction is thermodynamically favored, and how does a battery turn that free energy into electrical work?
objectives: Calculate ΔS for phase changes and heating with ΔS = q/T, and explain the sign at the particle level.
Calculate ΔS°rxn from standard molar entropies and ΔG°rxn from ΔG°f values.
Use ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° to decide when a reaction is favored, and find the crossover temperature.
Relate E°cell, ΔG° and K (ΔG° = −nFE°, ΔG° = −RT ln K) and use the Nernst equation.
Distinguish galvanic and electrolytic cells and use q = It and Faraday's constant to find the mass plated.
materials: A short table of standard reduction potentials (optional)
prep: **The Unit 9 labs are not on the ChemSims site's sim list, the sim's home page, or its menu**, so they can't be assigned through the site. Post these four links for students: chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=91, ?part=92, ?part=93, ?part=94. If a student presses Home or uses the ☰ menu, they land in the Unit 6 labs; they must reopen the link.
Run each lab once in Guided mode with the worksheet's settings: Part 91 with water at 7 g; Part 93 with the four slider values in the Set Up box; Part 94 with Zn/Cu, 5.0 A and 1800 s.
Part 94 has 49 screens and three drag steps (voltmeter, thermometer, power source). Check that dragging works on your students' devices; on a touchscreen the drag can be fiddly.

The sim doesn't cover 9.4 kinetic control (beyond one sentence) or 9.6 coupled reactions. Use your usual lesson for them (e.g., diamond → graphite for kinetic control; ATP hydrolysis or the smelting of metal oxides with carbon for coupling).
Decide before day 6 whether students self-grade or you grade (see the shared grading section).
prior_knowledge: q = mcΔT, heat of fusion/vaporization and heating curves (Unit 6).
Enthalpy of reaction from formation values (Unit 6).
Q vs. K and Le Châtelier's principle (Unit 7).

days.title: Teacher demo: entropy and melting
days.goal: Introduce entropy and ΔS = q/T, and model how to record sim data on the worksheet.
agenda: Warm-up: "Which has more ways to arrange its particles: an ice cube or a puddle?"
Demo of Part 91, slides 1–17 (script below); students fill in pp. 1–2
Pairs finish the calculation and question
Exit check: ΔSₘₑₗₜ for 15 g (18 J/K)

demo_script.do: Project chemsims.app/sims/thermodynamics?part=91. Point out the tab title "Unit 9: Applications of Thermodynamics" and the Guided tab.
demo_script.say: This lab is only reachable by this link, so bookmark it.

demo_script.do: Press Next through slides 1–3 (First Law, Second Law).
demo_script.say: What does "cannot be transferred with 100% efficiency" mean for a car engine? (Expected: some energy always ends up as waste heat.)

demo_script.do: Press Next through slides 4–7 (balls in a box).
demo_script.say: If the box gets smaller, do the balls have more or fewer places to be? (Fewer → entropy decreases.)
The sim writes J/°C. We'll write J/K. Why are the numbers the same? (A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size.)

demo_script.do: On slide 9, open Choose a Substance and pick Water. Press Next through slides 10–12.
demo_script.say: ΔS = q/T. Why must T be in kelvin? (Dividing by 0 °C would be impossible; entropy is measured from absolute zero.)

demo_script.do: Point to Ice mass: 7 g. Ask students to predict the sign of ΔS for melting.
demo_script.say: Write your prediction before I touch the flame. (Expected: positive.)

demo_script.do: Show the fusion equation (2331 / 273 = 7(333) / 273). Pause: have students calculate ΔSₘₑₗₜ.
demo_script.say: The sim says the heat of fusion is 333 J/g. Calculate q and ΔSₘₑₗₜ now. (2331 J, 273 K, 9 J/K.)

demo_script.do: Move the Heat slider slowly through the melting plateau. Stop when the bubble reads "Entropy increased by 9 J/°C".
demo_script.say: The thermometer never moved. So where did the entropy come from? (Heat broke up the solid's order.)

demo_script.do: Point at the graph at the top: it shows temperature vs. energy, not entropy.
demo_script.say: The bubble says the change is noticeable in the graph, but this graph shows temperature. The entropy number is in the equation panel.

demo_script.do: Stop at the end of melting. Do not go on to heating the liquid.
demo_script.say: Tomorrow you'll finish the heating curve yourselves and compare three substances.

misconceptions.sim_fix: Part 93 round 3 is exothermic (ΔH° = −5000 J/mol) but has ΔG° = +120 J/mol at 320 K; it only becomes favored when cooled.

misconceptions.misconception: A negative ΔG° means the reaction is fast.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Part 93's second intro slide: "That does not tell you how fast it occurs; even a favorable reaction can be very slow."

misconceptions.misconception: A negative ΔG° means the reaction goes to completion.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Round 3's ΔG° = −232 J/mol gives K ≈ 1.1; the round 2–3 closer says a real mixture would stop partway, at equilibrium.

misconceptions.misconception: Temperature has no effect on entropy unless there is a phase change.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Part 91's heating legs add entropy (9 J/K for heating 7 g of liquid water from 0 to 100 °C) with no change of state.
Part 94 says electrons flow from the negative side (anode) to the positive side (cathode) in the galvanic cell.

sim_cautions: The Unit 9 labs open only from the direct link. The ☰ menu and Home lead to the Unit 6 labs, and the "Next chapter" button at the end of Part 91 opens the Unit 6 bond enthalpy lab, not Part 92.
Part 91 calls water's heat of vaporization the "Heat of Fusion" at the start of boiling, and says the 42 J/°C was "for the melting process". Both are about boiling.
Part 91 says the entropy change is "more noticeable in the graph at the top", but that graph shows temperature, not entropy.
Part 92 says ΔG°f is in J and the beaker callout labels S° values (like 191.5) as kJ. Entropies are J/K·mol and Gibbs energies are kJ/mol.

Part 92's last slide says ΔG is negative "because the reaction is spontaneous". It's the other way around: a negative ΔG° is what tells us it is favored. For NaOH it also gives the reason "all gaseous", but Na and NaOH are solids.
Part 93's beaker shows all-or-nothing reactions. Rounds 2 and 3 have K ≈ 1.05–1.10, so a real mixture would be only partly converted.
In Part 94, use Zn/Cu. The Al/Ag reaction mislabels Ag⁺ as Ag³⁺ and leaves the cube off [Ag⁺] in Q.
Part 94 reads E° for zinc as "0.76" with no minus sign; the equation strip shows the correct −0.76.

Part 94's electrolysis text says the grams of Cu consumed equal the grams of Zn plated (only the moles are equal) and that the zinc electrode is coated "with Zn²⁺ ions" (it is coated with zinc metal).

exit_ticket.question: A reaction has ΔH° = +5000 J/mol and ΔS° = +16 J/(mol·K). Is it favored at 298 K? At 320 K?
exit_ticket.answer: No at 298 K (ΔG° = +232 J/mol); yes at 320 K (ΔG° = −120 J/mol). It is favored above 312.5 K.

exit_ticket.question: A cell has E°cell = +1.10 V and n = 2. What is the sign of ΔG°, and is K greater or less than 1?
How many grams of Zn are plated by 9000 C?

ap_practice.question: Multiple choice. For a reaction, ΔH° = −5000 J/mol and ΔS° = −16 J/(mol·K). Which is true? (A) Favored at all temperatures. (B) Favored only below 312.5 K. (C) Favored only above 312.5 K. (D) Never favored.
ap_practice.answer: (B). ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is negative only while |ΔH°| > T|ΔS°|, i.e. T < 5000/16 = 312.5 K (Part 93, round 3).

ap_practice.question: FRQ. A galvanic cell is built from Zn(s) in 1.00 M Zn²⁺ and Cu(s) in 1.00 M Cu²⁺ at 298 K. E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. (a) Write the anode half-reaction. (b) Calculate E°cell. (c) Calculate ΔG° in kJ/mol rxn. (d) More Zn(NO₃)₂ is dissolved in the anode beaker. Does Ecell increase, decrease or stay the same? Justify with Q. (e) The cell is then recharged as an electrolytic cell at 5.0 A for 1800 s. Calculate the mass of Zn deposited.
ap_practice.answer: (a) Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. (b) 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. (c) ΔG° = −(2)(96485)(1.10) = −2.12 × 10⁵ J = −212 kJ/mol rxn. (d) Decreases: [Zn²⁺] is in the numerator of Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺], so Q increases and Ecell = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q goes down. (e) q = 9000 C; 0.0933 mol e⁻; 0.0466 mol Zn; 3.05 g Zn.
